lead: Exergy is the useful work a system or stream can still give as it comes to equilibrium with the surroundings. The surroundings are at T₀ and p₀, called the dead state. At the dead state a system has zero exergy. Exergy analysis shows where useful work is lost: every irreversibility destroys exergy equal to T₀ times the entropy generated. Power plants, turbines, heat exchangers and refrigeration units use this to compare real performance with the best possible performance, not merely with the first law energy balance.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the dead state and T₀ΔS, and Unit 3 for entropy generation in an adiabatic device.

sections.h3: Dead state and exergy of a system or stream

blocks.text: The dead state is the state of the environment: temperature T₀, pressure p₀. A system at the dead state cannot produce work by interacting with the environment. Exergy is the maximum useful work a system can deliver as it moves reversibly from its present state to the dead state, exchanging heat only with the environment at T₀. Some syllabi call exergy availability.
Φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀)
blocks.where: Φ is specific exergy in kJ/kg; u is specific internal energy; v is specific volume; s is specific entropy; subscript 0 is the dead state; T₀ and p₀ are dead-state temperature and pressure.

blocks.text: For a closed system of mass m kg, the total exergy is mΦ kJ, and Φ is the specific exergy in kJ/kg. Here u is specific internal energy in kJ/kg, v is specific volume in m³/kg, s is specific entropy in kJ/kg·K. The term p₀(v − v₀) is work done against the environment; the last term subtracts the heat that must be dumped to the environment.

blocks.where: ψ is flow exergy in kJ/kg; h is specific enthalpy; s is specific entropy; subscript 0 is the dead state; T₀ is the dead-state temperature in kelvin.

blocks.text: For a flowing stream, the exergy per kg is ψ. Flow exergy does not contain a p₀v term because the environment already pushes the stream in and out. A stream at the dead state has ψ = 0. Absolute values of h and s are not needed; only changes from the dead state appear. For a steady adiabatic device, the exergy supplied by the stream is ψ₁ − ψ₂. This drop is the maximum work the device could give. It is larger than the actual work when the process is irreversible.

Write an exergy balance for any steady device: exergy in − exergy out − I = 0. I is the exergy destroyed, also called irreversibility in some syllabi. For a turbine with adiabatic flow, ψ₁ − ψ₂ − w − I = 0, so w = ψ₁ − ψ₂ − I. The work is always less than the exergy drop.

blocks.where: I is exergy destroyed, in kJ for a mass m, in kJ/kg for unit mass, in kW for a steady stream; also called irreversibility in some syllabi.
I is exergy destroyed; T₀ is dead-state temperature in K; S_gen is entropy generated: S_gen in kJ/kg·K gives I in kJ/kg, S_gen in kW/K gives I in kW.

blocks.text: The Gouy-Stodola theorem gives I = T₀ S_gen. T₀ is the environment temperature in kelvin, S_gen is the entropy generated in kJ/kg·K for a unit mass, so I is in kJ/kg. For an adiabatic device, S_gen = s₂ − s₁. For a device with heat transfer, include the entropy change of the reservoirs that exchange heat. Exergy is not conserved; it is destroyed by friction, mixing, finite-temperature heat transfer, and throttling.

Why T₀? Entropy generation represents energy that has become unavailable. Multiplying by T₀ converts that entropy to the equivalent work that can no longer be obtained. Chapter 4.1 available and unavailable energy uses the same product T₀ΔS.
The figure shows the bookkeeping. Exergy enters with the stream. Part leaves as useful work, and the rest is destroyed. The destroyed part is not a stream; it has left the exergy account.

sections.h3: Second law efficiency, not isentropic efficiency

blocks.text: Second law efficiency compares what we get with the best possible. It is η_II = exergy recovered ÷ exergy supplied. A reversible device has η_II = 1. A real device has η_II < 1.

blocks.where: η_II is second law efficiency; both exergy terms use the same units and the same dead state.
w is actual work out in kJ/kg; ψ₁ and ψ₂ are flow exergies at inlet and outlet in kJ/kg.

blocks.text: Do not confuse η_II with isentropic efficiency. Isentropic efficiency uses only the enthalpy drop to the same exit pressure; second law efficiency uses the exergy drop, which carries T₀(s₂ − s₁). For an adiabatic turbine that expands entirely above T₀, the entropy is generated at temperatures above T₀, so T₀·S_gen is less than the isentropic lost work and η_II comes out higher than η_is. The two numbers are different measures; always check which one the question asks for.

blocks.where: Δψ_cold is exergy gained by the cold stream; Δψ_hot is exergy lost by the hot stream, both in kW.

blocks.text: For a heat exchanger, exergy is supplied by the hot stream as it cools: Δψ_hot = ψ_h,in − ψ_h,out. Exergy is recovered by the cold stream: Δψ_cold = ψ_c,out − ψ_c,in. If the hot stream gives 200 kW of exergy and the cold stream receives 150 kW, η_II = 150/200 = 0.75, and 50 kW is destroyed. A reversible heat exchanger with no temperature difference would have equal exergy changes, but real heat transfer across a finite temperature difference destroys exergy.

figure.caption: The stream supplies 660 kJ/kg of exergy. The turbine converts 600 kJ/kg to work and destroys 60 kJ/kg, equal to T₀S_gen.

spec.title: Exergy balance of a steady-flow device
spec.aria: A stream supplies 660 kJ/kg of exergy to a turbine, which delivers 600 kJ/kg as work while 60 kJ/kg is destroyed and equals T0 times the entropy generated.

examples.question: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.80 kJ/kg·K and leaves at h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg, s₂ = 7.00 kJ/kg·K. The dead state is at T₀ = 300 K. Find the work per kg, the exergy destroyed and the second law efficiency. Take no heat loss.
steps: Energy balance for the adiabatic turbine gives w = h₁ − h₂ = 3200 − 2600 = 600 kJ/kg.
Entropy generation for the adiabatic device is S_gen = s₂ − s₁ = 7.00 − 6.80 = 0.20 kJ/kg·K.
Exergy destroyed is I = T₀ S_gen = 300 K × 0.20 kJ/kg·K = 60 kJ/kg.
Stream exergy drop is ψ₁ − ψ₂ = (h₁ − h₂) − T₀(s₁ − s₂) = 600 − 300 × (6.80 − 7.00) = 600 + 60 = 660 kJ/kg. The same value is w + I = 600 + 60 = 660 kJ/kg.
Second law efficiency is η_II = w/(ψ₁ − ψ₂) = 600/660 = 0.9091, about 0.909 or 90.9%.
examples.answer: The work is 600 kJ/kg, the exergy destroyed is 60 kJ/kg, and the second law efficiency is 0.909, about 90.9%.
examples.check:
h1 = 3200.0
s1 = 6.80
h2 = 2600.0
s2 = 7.00
T0 = 300.0
w = h1 - h2
sgen = s2 - s1
I = T0 * sgen
drop = w + I
eta = w / drop
print(round(w, 3))
print(round(sgen, 3))
print(round(I, 3))
print(round(drop, 3))
print(round(eta, 3))

traps: Using isentropic efficiency as second law efficiency. Isentropic efficiency uses h₁ − h₂s; second law efficiency uses ψ₁ − ψ₂.
Dropping the T₀Δs term and calling the enthalpy drop the exergy drop. For a turbine, ψ₁ − ψ₂ = (h₁ − h₂) − T₀(s₁ − s₂).
Using 298 K when the question gives T₀ = 300 K. Use the stated dead-state temperature.
Writing S_gen = s₁ − s₂ for an adiabatic device. Entropy generation is positive, s₂ − s₁.
Treating destroyed exergy as a stream leaving the device. It is a loss in the balance, not a flow.

quiz.a: The state of the environment, at temperature T₀ and pressure p₀, where a system has zero exergy.

quiz.q: Write the flow exergy per kg.
quiz.a: ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀), with h enthalpy, s entropy, subscript 0 dead state.

quiz.q: Why is destroyed exergy equal to T₀S_gen?
quiz.a: Entropy generation measures energy made unavailable; multiplying by the environment temperature T₀ converts it to the equivalent lost work.

quiz.q: Steam in an adiabatic turbine: h₁ = 3000 kJ/kg, h₂ = 2500 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.50 kJ/kg·K, s₂ = 6.80 kJ/kg·K, T₀ = 300 K. Find w, I, ψ₁ − ψ₂ and η_II.
A turbine has isentropic efficiency 0.90 and second law efficiency 0.93. Is this possible? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes. η_is compares actual work with the isentropic enthalpy drop; η_II compares actual work with the stream exergy drop w + T₀·S_gen. Because the entropy is generated at temperatures above T₀, T₀·S_gen is smaller than the isentropic lost work, so η_II > η_is. The two must not be interchanged.

quiz.q: In a heat exchanger the hot stream loses 200 kW of exergy and the cold stream gains 150 kW. Find η_II and the exergy destroyed.
For adiabatic throttling, h is constant and s rises. What happens to exergy?
quiz.a: ψ₁ − ψ₂ = T₀(s₂ − s₁), all of it is destroyed; no work is produced. The throttling process has η_II = 0 for work recovery.

quiz.q: Why is exergy not conserved in a real device?
quiz.a: Friction, mixing, finite-temperature heat transfer and throttling generate entropy, and T₀S_gen destroys exergy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Exergy analysis is used in power plant audits, heat exchanger network design and building energy studies. Exergoeconomics puts a price on exergy destruction, so a rupee of lost work is charged to the equipment that causes it. Data-centre cooling and district heating use second law efficiency to compare heat recovery options. Search 'exergy analysis', 'Gouy-Stodola' and 'exergoeconomics' to go further.
